walkthroughs.title: Meet Aeriocode, your new coding partner
walkthroughs.description: Aeriocode codes like a developer because it thinks like one. Here are 5 ways to put it to work:

steps.description: Point Aeriocode to your project. It builds understanding to make smart, context-aware changes.

steps.title: Always Use the Best AI Models
steps.description: Aeriocode empowers you with State-of-the-Art AI, connecting to top models (Anthropic, Gemini, OpenAI & more).

steps.title: You're Always in Control
steps.description: Review Aeriocode's plans and diffs. Approve changes before they happen. No surprises.

enumDescriptions: Off. No coding standard is enforced and Aeriocode behaves as an ordinary assistant.

Aerio Safety Coding Standard - 158 rules, 137 checked automatically, covering C, C++, Ada and Rust. Adoptable as a programme's Software Code Standards under DO-178C 11.8, including eight rules constraining AI-assisted authoring under 11.8(e).
aeriocode.compliance.standard.markdownDescription:
The coding standard Aeriocode holds generated code to. **Off by default** - set it per workspace so a certified repository and an internal tool can differ without you having to remember which is selected.

When set, generated code is analysed after every write and violations are returned to the model to fix. This is not a certification and does not guarantee one: Aerio reports findings, and whether the evidence suffices is decided by the applicant and their certification authority.

enumDescriptions: Airborne software. Levels are DO-178C design assurance levels A to D.
Space software, European. Levels are ECSS software criticality categories A to D, per ECSS-Q-ST-80C Annex D.
Space software, NASA. Levels are NASA software classifications A to F, per NPR 7150.2D Appendix E. Class F is business and IT software, not the bottom of the scale.

Not available. Aerio holds no copy of ISO 26262 and asserts no mapping from these rules to ASILs, so no level applies and the standard is applied in full. Recognised so an existing setting is not silently rewritten, but not offered in the picker.
aeriocode.compliance.regime.markdownDescription:
Which assurance regime the level below is expressed in.

**DO-178C, ECSS and NASA each carry a projection. ISO 26262 does not and is not offered** - Aerio holds no copy of it and will not acquire one for this product, so it would apply the standard in full and change nothing you could observe. It stays in this list only so a workspace that already has it set is not silently rewritten to DO-178C.

The three projections are shaped differently, because the regimes are. DO-178C's levels differ in how much verification evidence they demand, so the projection grades rules down at the lower levels. ECSS instead requires the coding standard you declared to be observed at every criticality category and tailors that clause nowhere, so the ECSS projection is flat - only three process rules about naming tools in the plan are not applicable at category D. NASA is flat again but over six classifications, and its variation is about generated code rather than consequence: the requirement covering automatically generated source stops at class C, so the eight rules governing AI-assisted authoring do not apply at class D and return at class F.

**No rule of the standard applies at NASA class E.** That is NPR 7150.2D's own position - it asks no coding or verification requirement of class E software at all - not Aerio relaxing anything.

Three of these regimes label their levels A-D and mean three different things by them: an ECSS criticality category is a function's severity category *modulated by* whether a compensating provision exists outside the software, a DO-178C design assurance level is a failure condition classification with no such modulation, and a NASA class is assigned from the kind of mission the software serves. No publisher defines a mapping between any two of them, and Aerio does not convert.

enumDescriptions: Not assigned. The standard is applied in full, which is the stricter reading.
DO-178C level A, ECSS category A, or NASA class A.
DO-178C level B, ECSS category B, NASA class B, or ISO 26262 ASIL B.
DO-178C level C, ECSS category C, NASA class C, or ISO 26262 ASIL C.
DO-178C level D, ECSS category D, NASA class D, or ISO 26262 ASIL D.
NASA class E only. NPR 7150.2D asks no coding requirement of class E software, so no rule of the standard is applied.
NASA class F only - general-purpose computing, business and IT software. Not the bottom of the scale: it carries the coding-standard requirement class E does not.
aeriocode.compliance.level.markdownDescription:
The integrity level this software is being developed to: a DO-178C design assurance level (A, B, C, D), an ECSS software criticality category (A, B, C, D), a NASA software classification (A to F), or an ISO 26262 ASIL (D, C, B, A, QM). Which of those the letter means is decided by the regime above.

Leave empty if you have not been assigned one - the standard is then applied in full, which is the stricter reading. A level should be set from the system safety assessment or the project's software classification, not chosen for convenience: it is a claim about how much assurance the software needs.

**E and F belong to the NASA regime only.** A level that does not belong to the selected regime is dropped and reported rather than applied, because silently ignoring it would relax the standard without saying so.

aeriocode.compliance.gateEnabled.markdownDescription:
Analyse generated code after every write and return violations to the model to fix.

Only has effect when a standard is set. Turning it off leaves the system prompt telling the model to follow the standard with nothing checking that it did - which is the difference between steering and verification.

scripts.compile: npm run check-types && npm run lint && node esbuild.mjs
scripts.compile-standalone: npm run check-types && npm run lint && node esbuild.mjs --standalone
scripts.package: npm run check-types && npm run build:webview && npm run lint && node esbuild.mjs --production
scripts.postprotos: prettier src/shared/proto src/core/controller src/hosts/ webview-ui/src/services --write --log-level warn && [ -d src/generated ] && prettier src/generated --write --log-level warn || true
scripts.clean: rimraf dist dist-standalone webview-ui/build src/generated out/
scripts.check-types: npm run protos && npx tsc --noEmit && cd webview-ui && npx tsc -b --noEmit
scripts.lint: cross-env ESLINT_USE_FLAT_CONFIG=false eslint src --ext ts && cross-env ESLINT_USE_FLAT_CONFIG=false eslint webview-ui/src --ext ts && buf lint && cd webview-ui && npm run lint
scripts.pretest: npm run compile && npm run compile-tests && npm run compile-standalone && npm run lint
scripts.test:e2e: playwright install && vsce package --no-dependencies --out dist/e2e.vsix && node src/test/e2e/utils/build.js && playwright test
scripts.test:e2e:optimal: vsce package --no-dependencies --out dist/e2e.vsix && node src/test/e2e/utils/build.js && playwright test
scripts.install:all: npm install && cd webview-ui && npm install
